title: STARDUST: A pipeline for the unbiased analysis of astrocyte regional calcium dynamics
author: Wu, Dai, et al.

steps.title: Motion‑correct raw recordings
steps.instruction: Using MATLAB and the NoRMCorre plugin, apply motion correction to the raw GCaMP and tdTomato .tif recordings (steps 1‑3 of Part 1). Save the motion‑corrected GCaMP file as “motion‑corrected GCaMP recording.tif” and the motion‑corrected tdTomato file as “motion‑corrected tdTomato recording.tif” (the tdTomato file should receive the same transformation as the GCaMP file).

steps.title: Detect active pixels with AQuA
steps.instruction: In MATLAB run AQuA on the motion‑corrected GCaMP .tif (steps 4‑13 of Part 2). Export the AQuA overlay video as “AQuA overlay video.tif” and the MATLAB project file as “AQuA.mat”.

steps.title: Export ROA masks from AQuA
steps.instruction: Open the AQuA overlay video in ImageJ (steps 14‑17 of Part 3) and export the ROA set as a zip file “ROA RoiSet.zip” and the binary mask as “ROA mask.tif”.

steps.title: Extract ROA fluorescence time‑series
steps.instruction: Using ImageJ (steps 18‑21 of Part 4), load the motion‑corrected GCaMP .tif and the ROA mask.tif, then extract the fluorescence intensity time‑series for each ROA. Save the results as “time series.csv” and also export the ROA RoiSet.zip (same as above).

steps.title: Generate cell segmentation mask
steps.instruction: In ImageJ (steps 22‑25 of Part 5), load the motion‑corrected tdTomato .tif, segment individual astrocyte somata, and export the cell set as a zip file “Cell RoiSet.zip” and the binary mask as “Cell mask.tif”.

steps.title: Download and extract STARDUST repository
steps.instruction: From https://github.com/papouinlab/STARDUST click the green “Code” button, choose “Download ZIP”, and save the zip file to the C: drive (recommended). Extract all files to a local directory.

substeps.instruction: a. Open the GitHub page and click the green “Code” → “Download ZIP”.
b. Save the zip file to a folder on the C: drive (e.g., C:\STARDUST‑main).
c. Extract the zip archive, preserving the folder structure.

steps.title: Create dedicated conda environment (optional)
steps.instruction: Import the provided YAML file (STARDUSTreq.yml) into Anaconda Navigator to create an isolated environment with the required module versions.

substeps.instruction: b. Click “Import”, ensure “Local drive” is selected, and browse to the extracted STARDUST‑main folder to choose “STARDUSTreq.yml”.
c. Optionally rename the new environment.
d. Click “Import” to create the environment.

steps.title: Launch appropriate Jupyter Notebook
steps.instruction: From the Anaconda Navigator home page launch Jupyter Notebook, navigate to the extracted STARDUST‑main folder, and open the notebook that matches the desired analysis type:

substeps.instruction: a. For cell‑assigned ROA analysis open “STARDUST.ipynb”.
b. For ROA‑based analysis open “STARDUST ROA‑based.ipynb”.
c. For cell‑based analysis open “STARDUST cell‑based.ipynb”.

steps.title: Import Python modules and utilities
steps.instruction: Run the first code block in the notebook to import pandas, numpy, seaborn, scipy, matplotlib, PIL and all custom functions from src/STARDUST/util.py.

steps.title: Verify module versions
steps.instruction: Execute the code block `check_modules()` to confirm that the installed packages match the required versions.

steps.title: Provide input paths and experiment metadata
steps.instruction: Run the code block that calls `prompt_input()` and `get_metadata()`. When prompted, enter:

substeps.instruction: • Path to the folder containing the three required input files (time series.csv, ROA mask.tif, cell mask.tif).

steps.title: Load ROA and cell masks
steps.instruction: Execute `read_tif(ROA_mask_path, "ROA")` and `read_tif(cell_mask_path, "cell")` to obtain the mask arrays, labeled maps, and counts. Verify that the reported numbers of ROAs and cells match those generated in ImageJ.

steps.title: Visualize masks (optional)
steps.instruction: If desired, run `visualize_map(ROA_map_array=ROA_map_array, cell_map_array=cell_map_array)` to display the ROA and cell segmentation overlays.

steps.title: Extract signal features
steps.instruction: Run the code block `signal_features = analyze_signal(dff_traces, signal_frames, signal_boundaries, frame_rate, drug_frame)`. This computes for each detected signal the start/end frames, times, peak frame, AUC, amplitude, SNR, rise/decay times, half‑width, duration, inter‑event interval, and epoch classification (baseline/drug). Expected runtime ≈ 30 s.

steps.title: Perform ROA‑based analysis
steps.instruction: Execute `ROA_based, ROA_info = ROA_analysis(signal_features, ROA_info, frame_count, frame_rate, drug_frame, cell_segmentation=True)`. The function summarizes average signal features per ROA, computes frequency per minute, and categorizes each ROA as “stable”, “on”, “off”, “inactive”, or “NA”. Expected runtime ≈ 1 min.

steps.title: Perform cell‑assigned ROA analysis
steps.instruction: Run `cell_assigned = cell_analysis(signal_features, ROA_info)`. This assigns each ROA to its corresponding cell and generates a table where each row represents a cell with summarized ROA activity features. Expected runtime ≈ 1 min.

description: Astrocytes, a main type of non-neuronal cells, display fluctuations of intracellular calcium concentrations ([Ca2+]i) that are responsive to ambient conditions and neuroactive molecules.1,2,3 Fluorescence imaging of Ca2+ indicators is thus a popular means to probe astrocyte activity in vitro, ex vivo and in vivo.1,2,3 Proven methods of neuronal Ca2+ imaging and analysis have been widely adapted to astrocytes for this purpose. However, important differences between neurons and astrocytes mean that key operational assumptions are not transferable. For instance, in neurons, Ca2+ activity is driven by depolarization-induced transmembrane Ca2+ fluxes. By contrast, the origins and mechanisms of astrocytes Ca2+ signals are diverse and still largely elusive, limiting our ability to functionally interpret Ca2+ events. Astrocytic [Ca2+]i fluctuations also primarily occur outside of the soma, within highly localized micro/nano-domains, and seldom propagate or merge at the cell body.4,5,6,7 Concomitantly, the complexity of astrocyte morphology and its sub-diffraction limit scale also make it difficult to register areas of Ca2+ activity to identifiable morphological features in live fluorescence imaging. Hence, there is a growing need to enrich the astrocyte Ca2+ toolbox with analysis methods tailored to astrocytes. Owing to the constrains listed above, such methods need to be 1) holistic, to capture all activities in the cell, 2) unbiased, rather than restricted to user-defined regions of interest, 3) agnostic, to make no or minimal assumptions regarding the rules of Ca2+ propagation or integration, and 4) with instrument-limited accuracy, to favor detailed investigations consistent with the nanoscale nature of astrocytes architecture.8 Here, we introduce STARDUST, a pipeline that captures Ca2+ dynamics in confined, local micro-domains across the territory of all astrocytes in 2-photon imaging recordings. STARDUST builds upon AQuA, a popular open-source platform,9 to yield maps
